p: Of 262 men who charged, 224 were casualties — 85.5%. It remains the highest casualty rate suffered by any Union regiment in a single engagement in the entire war.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The First Minnesota”, paragraph 11 of 12

p: The survivors — 38 men — formed in line the next morning and were ordered to hold the same ground. They did.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The First Minnesota”, paragraph 12 of 12

p: The orders came at dusk: Slocum was pulling the XII Corps south to reinforce the crumbling Union left. The brigades would move — all of them. All except Greene's.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Greene's Lone Stand”, paragraph 1 of 9

p: Brigadier General George Greene was sixty-two years old, the oldest brigade commander at Gettysburg. He was a West Point engineer who had spent his career building aqueducts and railroads. His five New York regiments — 1,424 men — were to hold Culp's Hill while the rest of the corps departed.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Greene's Lone Stand”, paragraph 2 of 9

p: Greene looked at his line. His five regiments normally occupied perhaps 600 yards of front. The entire XII Corps position was more than 1,300 yards. He was being asked to hold more than double his normal front — with the same number of men — against Johnson's Confederate division of 6,500.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Greene's Lone Stand”, paragraph 3 of 9

p: Greene had spent his career as an engineer. He understood defensive works. During the afternoon, while the army was fighting in the south, he had ordered his men to build breastworks — proper log-and-earth fortifications, not just scratched rifle pits. His officers had thought it excessive. Now those breastworks would save his command.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Greene's Lone Stand”, paragraph 4 of 9

p: Greene extended his line by thinning it beyond any conventional military standard. A man here, a man there, a twenty-foot gap between. The works did the work that bodies could not.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Greene's Lone Stand”, paragraph 5 of 9

p: Johnson's division attacked in waves. The Stonewall Brigade, Jones's brigade, Nicholls's brigade — all came up the dark hill into the abatis and the fire from Greene's thin line.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Greene's Lone Stand”, paragraph 6 of 9

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Greene's Lone Stand”, paragraph 7 of 9

p: For three hours, 1,424 men held Culp's Hill against 6,500. Steuart's brigade, on the Confederate left, found the empty XII Corps works and occupied them — but they could not advance past Greene's position. The upper hill stayed Union.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Greene's Lone Stand”, paragraph 8 of 9

p: When the XII Corps returned in the darkness, they found Greene still holding, his line still unbroken. He had lost 303 men. He had saved the Union right flank.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Greene's Lone Stand”, paragraph 9 of 9

p: The Louisiana Tigers had a reputation. In an army of hard men they were considered especially dangerous — New Orleans toughs, dock workers, immigrants, men with nothing to lose. Their officers sometimes controlled them with threats of summary execution. On the battlefield, they were formidable.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The Louisiana Tigers on Cemetery Hill”, paragraph 1 of 9

p: At dusk on July 2, Hays's five Louisiana regiments and Avery's three North Carolina regiments stepped off from the town of Gettysburg and began climbing Cemetery Hill.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The Louisiana Tigers on Cemetery Hill”, paragraph 2 of 9

p: The timing was not accidental. The Union artillery on the hill could not depress their guns enough to fire directly at men climbing the steep slope below them. The light was failing. The Confederate attack would have to be met with musketry alone.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The Louisiana Tigers on Cemetery Hill”, paragraph 3 of 9

p: Hays's men swept up the hill with a ferocity that overwhelmed the XI Corps units defending the lower slope. They reached the crest. They seized the Union guns. For a few minutes — perhaps ten, perhaps fifteen — Louisiana and North Carolina men stood on the summit of Cemetery Hill with Union artillery in their hands.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The Louisiana Tigers on Cemetery Hill”, paragraph 4 of 9

p: On the slope below, Colonel Isaac Avery was shot through the neck. He knew he was dying. Unable to speak, he found a pencil and a scrap of paper and wrote with a shaking hand: 'Tell my father I died with my face to the enemy.'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The Louisiana Tigers on Cemetery Hill”, paragraph 5 of 9
